fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me explain how I think about it, because I think about everything in terms of supply and demand, and a stock market is no different from any other market in that regard.

A bubble is a situation where prices are high relative to the traditional measures of value, where the purchases are being made with leverage, where new buyers are coming into the market who weren't there before, and where there's a broad bullish sentiment. Those are the classic ingredients, and I've measured them going back to 1900. And one of the things that happens in that environment is that it becomes very attractive to issue new stock. If I'm a company and my shares are trading at a very high price, or if I'm a private company and I see the valuations in the public market, I want to sell shares. I want to take advantage of that. So you get a lot of IPOs, you get a lot of secondary offerings, you get the SPACs, you get all these vehicles for creating new supply. It's the smart money selling to the enthusiastic money.

So what you have is this dynamic. On the demand side, the buying is coming largely from people who are extrapolating the past, who are buying because the price went up, and who are often borrowing to do it. That's a finite pool. On the supply side, every time the price goes up, more and more stock gets created to meet it. And at some point the supply of new shares exceeds the amount of new money coming in to buy them. That's when the thing turns. It's a very mechanical thing. You saw it in 1929, you saw it in 1999 and 2000, when the issuance of new technology companies got enormous relative to the buying power, and you saw a version of it in 2021.

And then what usually happens is that the central bank tightens, because the bubble is creating inflation or financial excess, and that reduces the liquidity that was funding the purchases. So you have less money chasing more stock. The leveraged buyers have to sell, which pushes prices down, which forces more selling. The pop is really that reversal, where supply and demand flip. The issuance by itself doesn't cause the pop, but it's one of the clearest signs that you're in the late stage, because it tells you that the people who know the most about what these businesses are worth would rather have the cash than the shares.

r001.rationale: The response says high prices encourage companies to issue shares through IPOs, secondary offerings, and SPACs, creating new stock supply.

r002.rationale: It explains that new shares can exceed incoming buying power and contribute to supply outstripping demand as a bubble turns, while clarifying issuance alone does not cause the pop.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, you have to think of it mechanically, because markets are just about buyers and sellers. Every time somebody buys a share, somebody else is selling it, and the price is determined by how much money comes in relative to the quantity of shares being offered. In a bubble, people tend to focus only on the demand side. They're excited, prices are going up, more money comes in, and that pushes prices up further. But they forget about the supply side.

When prices get high, there's a big incentive to create new supply. If you're a company and your stock is trading at a very high multiple, the smartest thing to do is sell stock, because you're getting a lot of money for very little. So you see a wave of IPOs and secondary offerings, and in some periods things like SPACs. Insiders and early investors who have been waiting want to cash out. Investment bankers are very happy to manufacture whatever the market wants to buy. So the quantity of stock out there goes up a lot.

Now, all of that new supply has to be absorbed by buyers, and buying it takes money. In a bubble a lot of that buying is financed with borrowed money, with leverage. At some point the amount of money needed to keep buying all that new paper exceeds the money that's available. Maybe the central bank tightens, maybe people just can't borrow more, maybe they need cash for something else. When there isn't enough money coming in to absorb what's being sold, prices have to fall.

Then you get the reversal of the self-reinforcing process. Prices fall, people who bought on leverage have to sell, which pushes prices down further, and the people who were selling stock at the top are the ones who did well. You saw this in 1929, and you saw it in the dot-com period in 2000, when there was an enormous amount of new issuance right at the top.

So one of the things I look at to gauge whether something is a bubble is how much new supply is being created. If a lot of companies are rushing to sell stock, and insiders are selling, that's a signal. The people who know the most about what the stock is worth are telling you something by what they're doing. It isn't a timing tool by itself, but it tells you the system is getting stretched, and that it will eventually need more money than is going to be there.

r001.rationale: It explains that high prices and strong demand make companies eager to issue stock, describing IPOs and secondary offerings as the resulting new supply.

r002.rationale: It says the increased supply must be absorbed by buyers and, when available money cannot absorb it, prices fall, contributing to the bubble’s reversal.

fable-5.text:
Well, the way to think about it is mechanically — everything that happens in markets is just buying and selling, supply and demand. A price is simply the amount of money spent divided by the quantity sold. So if you want to know whether a bubble will pop, you have to ask: where is the new buying going to come from, and where is the new supply coming from?

One of the classic markers of a bubble — and I've studied this going back hundreds of years, through 1929, through the dot-com period in 2000 — is that when prices get very high, it becomes very attractive to sell new stock. Companies see that they can raise money cheaply, so you get a flood of new issuance: IPOs, secondary offerings, new companies formed just to take advantage of the enthusiasm. Insiders and smart money sell to the new buyers coming in — often naive buyers, people who are buying not because of any calculation of value but because the price has been going up and they don't want to miss out, and often they're buying with borrowed money, with leverage.

So you have this dynamic where the supply of stock is increasing just as you're running out of new buyers. Everybody who was going to buy has largely bought. And the market needs ever more buying just to sustain the price — a bubble has to keep attracting new money or it falls under its own weight. When the issuance of new stock exceeds the amount of new money coming in to buy it, the price can't hold. Then, typically, you get a tightening of money and credit at the same time, because the central bank is responding to the strong conditions — and that's usually the pin. The leveraged buyers have to sell, the selling begets more selling, and the whole thing reverses.

So the new supply doesn't just contribute to the popping — it's one of the telltale signs you're in a bubble in the first place. When everyone wants to sell you new paper, and the buyers are new entrants using leverage, history says you should be careful.

r001.rationale: It says high prices make issuing stock attractive to companies, leading to a flood of new issuance.

r002.rationale: It explains that rising stock supply alongside fading new demand can exceed incoming money, causing prices to fall and the bubble to burst.

opus-5.text:
It's really a matter of arithmetic, and it's the part people pay the least attention to because it's not exciting. Think of the market as a machine with money coming in on one side and paper coming out on the other. When prices get high, the price is being held up by the flow of new money chasing a relatively fixed amount of stock. But high prices are an invitation. They're a signal to every company, every private owner, every venture investor, every banker, that this is a wonderful time to sell. And so the supply of paper starts to expand — IPOs, secondary offerings, insiders selling, convertible issuance, all of the vehicles that get invented at the top. In 1999 it was internet IPOs with no earnings. In 2021 it was the SPACs. The names change, the mechanism doesn't.

So what happens is you get to a point where the amount of new paper being issued exceeds the amount of new money coming in to buy it. And at that moment prices have to fall. Not because sentiment turned, not because there was bad news — the news usually comes after. It's just that the supply and demand changed, and the marginal buyer has already bought. Everybody who was going to come in has come in, often with borrowed money, and there's nobody left to sell to at that price.

That's why I watch new issuance as one of my bubble gauges, along with how much of the buying is leveraged and how many new, inexperienced buyers have entered. Issuance is the smart money telling you what it thinks, in the most honest way it can — with its own holdings. When the people who know the asset best are handing it to the people who know it least, and they're creating new supply to do it, you're late in the cycle. You don't know exactly when it breaks, but you know the mechanics are in place for it to break.

r001.rationale: It says money chasing a limited amount of stock supports high prices, which signal companies and other holders that it is a good time to sell and expand supply through issuance.

r002.rationale: It explains that when new stock issuance exceeds incoming money to buy it, prices fall because supply and demand have shifted.

sonnet-5.5.text:
It's really a supply and demand question, and it comes down to how much buying power there is relative to how much stock has to be absorbed.

In a bubble, prices are high relative to traditional measures of value, and a lot of the buying is financed with debt and speculation. That makes the market dependent on a continuing flow of new money. Then people who own the asset, or who can create it, see high prices and respond rationally. Companies issue more shares, insiders sell, private companies go public, and new vehicles get created to feed the appetite. We saw that in the late 1920s and in 2000, and we've seen versions of it more recently.

Each of those is a new supply of equity that somebody has to buy. As long as the money and credit keep flowing and sentiment is strong, the market absorbs it, and the rising prices encourage even more issuance. But it's a self-reinforcing process that has a limit. At some point the buyers have spent what they have, or borrowed what they can, and there's a lot of stock to be sold relative to the money available to buy it.

Then something tips the balance. Often it's tightening, meaning higher interest rates or less liquidity, because the central bank is worried about inflation or the excesses. That reduces buying power just as the supply is peaking. Prices stop rising, and the people who bought with leverage have to sell to meet their obligations or because they need cash. That adds more supply into a weaker market, and it feeds on itself in the other direction.

So I don't look at issuance alone. I look at how much supply is coming, how much buying power exists to absorb it, how much of that buying power is borrowed, and whether tightening is about to cut it off. A surge in new issuance when valuations are stretched and credit is about to tighten is one of the classic signs that you're late in the cycle.

r001.rationale: It says high prices and investor appetite lead companies to issue more shares and create new vehicles to feed demand.

r002.rationale: It explains that added stock supply can exceed available buying power, weakening prices and contributing to the bubble’s reversal.

haiku-5.5.text:
Think about it the way supply and demand always works. When prices are rising, the smartest thing a company can do is sell its own stock, because each share brings in more than it did a year earlier. So late in a bubble you see a wave of IPOs, secondary offerings, and companies using shares to buy other companies. New supply reaches the market just when buyers are most eager.

The money to absorb that supply is often borrowed, or it comes from people selling other assets to get in. When the marginal buyer runs out, or when credit tightens and people have to sell to repay loans, the new shares have no one to take them at those prices. That's when the cycle turns. Heavy selling by insiders is a signal too. When the people closest to a company are happy to issue and sell, the price is usually running ahead of what the cash flows can support.

So I wouldn't say new issuance pops the bubble by itself. It's a symptom of the bubble that becomes the mechanism once credit tightens and the buyers who were pushing prices up disappear.

r001.rationale: The response says companies issue stock when prices are rising, but it does not clearly state that investor demand encourages the creation and issuance of new stock.

r002.rationale: It says new shares become difficult to absorb when buyers disappear or credit tightens, making issuance part of the mechanism that turns the cycle.

astra-6.text:
Well, when stock prices get very high, it becomes attractive for companies to issue more stock. So the rising price itself brings out more supply, and that supply absorbs the money coming into the market.

At some point, there isn’t enough new buying to absorb all that stock at those prices. And remember, a lot of people are buying because prices have been going up. When prices stop rising, that reason for buying disappears. Some of those buyers become sellers, particularly if they’ve borrowed money and have to sell.

So you can get a reversal: more supply, less buying, falling prices—and those falling prices produce still more selling.

r001.rationale: The response says high stock prices make it attractive for companies to issue shares, but it does not clearly say investor demand encourages that issuance.

r002.rationale: It explains that additional stock supply can exceed available buying, contributing to falling prices and a reversal.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, when stock prices get very high, it becomes attractive for companies to issue more stock. And it becomes attractive to bring new companies to the market. So the rise in prices itself produces more supply.

Now, that supply has to be absorbed by somebody’s money. If you keep increasing the supply, eventually you can get beyond the demand that’s available at those prices. And remember, a lot of the demand in a bubble comes from people expecting prices to keep going up. When prices stop rising, that motivation changes. If they’ve borrowed money to buy, they may then have to sell.

So you can get a reinforcing process on the way down, just as you had on the way up. New issuance is one of the things I’d look at, together with who’s buying and how they’re financing those purchases.

r001.rationale: The response says high stock prices make issuance and bringing companies to market attractive, but does not clearly say investor demand encourages that new stock creation and issuance.

r002.rationale: The response explains that increased supply can exceed available demand at those prices and contribute to a reinforcing decline.

sol-6.text: When stock prices rise a lot, companies have an incentive to issue shares, and existing owners have an incentive to sell. That creates more supply for buyers to absorb. If the enthusiasm that drove prices up starts to fade, there may not be enough buyers at those prices. Prices fall, expectations change, and people who were counting on further gains begin to sell. So new issuance can help turn a bubble into a decline, though it’s usually part of a broader shift in demand and confidence.

r001.rationale: The response says high stock prices give companies an incentive to issue shares, but does not communicate that investor demand encourages the creation and issuance of new stock.

r002.rationale: It explains that new issuance adds supply for buyers to absorb and can help turn a bubble into a decline.

terra-5.6.text: When there’s a lot of new issuance, it’s a sign that people are eager to sell and companies are eager to take advantage of high prices. That adds supply into a market that may already be dependent on continued buying and credit. At some point, when the supply of stock exceeds the demand for it, prices start to fall—and that can become self-reinforcing as leveraged investors have to sell. So new issuance doesn’t by itself cause the bubble to pop, but it can be an important indicator that the market is becoming saturated.

r001.rationale: The response says companies issue stock to take advantage of high prices, but does not state that investor demand encourages the creation or issuance of new stock.

r002.rationale: It explains that excess stock supply can push prices down and trigger further selling, presenting increased supply as a contributor to a bubble bursting.

sol-5.6.text: It’s the basic supply-and-demand dynamic. In a bubble, rising prices attract buyers, and that demand encourages companies and existing shareholders to issue more stock. Eventually, the new supply becomes larger than the amount of money available to buy it. The market can no longer absorb all that issuance, prices begin to weaken, and leveraged investors are forced to sell. That shift—from demand exceeding supply to supply exceeding demand—is often what causes the bubble to pop.

r001.rationale: It says rising prices attract buyers and that this demand encourages companies and existing shareholders to issue more stock.

r002.rationale: It explains that new stock supply can exceed available buying money, weaken prices, and help cause the bubble to pop.

luna-5.6.text: When a market is in a bubble, there’s usually more demand for stocks than supply, so prices keep getting pushed up. But as companies begin issuing more shares—through IPOs, secondary offerings, or stock-based compensation—that supply can overwhelm the available buying power. If investors are already fully invested or borrowing heavily, there aren’t enough new buyers to absorb those shares. Prices then stop rising, and that can expose the leverage and optimism underneath the bubble, causing the decline to accelerate.

r001.rationale: The response says demand is high and companies begin issuing more shares, but does not communicate that investor demand encourages the creation or issuance of those shares.

r002.rationale: It explains that increased share issuance can overwhelm buying power, stop price increases, and accelerate a decline, making added stock supply a cause of the bubble bursting.

luna-6.text: New issuance adds to the supply of stocks investors have to absorb. When prices are high, companies and early investors have an incentive to sell more shares, so you often see a wave of IPOs and secondary offerings near a market peak. If demand can’t keep up with that new supply, prices come under pressure. And once prices start falling, investors who bought on leverage may have to sell too, which adds even more supply and can help the bubble unwind.

r001.rationale: The response says high prices encourage companies and early investors to sell shares, but does not say investor demand encourages new stock to be created and issued.

r002.rationale: It explains that new stock supply can outpace demand, pressure prices, and add to the forces that unwind a bubble.
